description: UDP versus TCP tail latency, by placement and offered rate
sql_code: -- Does UDP give a lower tail latency than TCP, and under what conditions?
-- udp_advantage_x is TCP's p99 divided by UDP's. Above 1 means UDP has the
-- lower tail, below 1 means it is worse.
-- At low offered rates the two are indistinguishable. UDP pulls ahead only
-- once the rate is high enough for TCP's congestion control to engage, and
-- Standard tuning only, so every provider is compared on the same
round(median(CASE WHEN protocol = 'tcp' THEN p99_rtt_us END) / 1000.0, 2) AS tcp_p99_ms,
round(median(CASE WHEN protocol = 'udp' THEN p99_rtt_us END) / 1000.0, 2) AS udp_p99_ms,
round(median(CASE WHEN protocol = 'tcp' THEN p99_rtt_us END)
/ nullif(median(CASE WHEN protocol = 'udp' THEN p99_rtt_us END), 0), 1) AS udp_advantage_x,
r_code: to_svg <- svgstring(width = output.width.inch, height = output.height.inch, scaling = 1)

output <- ggplot(df, aes(x = factor(offered_mps), y = udp_advantage_x, fill = placement_class)) +
geom_col(position = "dodge") +
geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
facet_wrap(~ provider) +
labs(x = "Offered rate (messages/s)",
y = "TCP p99 / UDP p99  (>1 means UDP is better)",
fill = "Placement") +
theme_bw() +
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
plot(output); dev.off(); to_svg() # output to the html page

description: Is UDP's tail advantage bought with loss?
sql_code: -- A lower tail only counts if the messages arrived. UDP can meet any offered
-- rate by discarding whatever the receiver cannot take, so its latency
-- figures have to be read next to how much of the load survived.
-- Read udp_delivered_pct first. Where it is below 100, the latency beside it
-- describes the messages that survived, not the load that was offered.

facet_wrap(~ placement_class) +
coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 105)) +
labs(x = "Offered rate (messages/s)", y = "UDP delivered (% of sent)", fill = "Provider") +
theme_bw()

description: Network-throughput tuning profile, standard versus tuned (STACKIT)
sql_code: -- Does a throughput-oriented sysctl profile help latency? It switches
-- congestion control, enlarges socket buffers and deepens queues.
-- congestion_control and rmem_max are read back from the machine after the
-- profile was applied, so the table shows the treatment that actually took
-- effect rather than the one requested.
-- Only one provider appears, because only one was measured under both
-- CPU steal is time the guest was ready to run but the hypervisor gave the
-- core to another tenant. It is the visible signature of a noisy neighbour.
-- The latency benchmark has the server echo every message, so a descheduled
-- server sits inside the round trip being measured. Contention and a genuine
-- transport effect look identical in a latency column.
-- A provider at 0% is uncontended; rows well above it are measuring the
-- hypervisor as much as the network.
JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT run_id, scenario_name, provider, client_machine_type
ON c.run_id = cpu.run_id AND c.scenario_name = cpu.scenario_name

sql_code: -- Where UDP loss actually happens. rb_bytes is the socket receive buffer the
-- kernel granted; queue_fill_ratio is how close the receive queue came to
-- Drops appearing as that ratio approaches 1 mean the loss is buffer limited:
-- the packets arrived and were discarded because the application could not
-- read them in time, not because the network dropped them.
-- rb_bytes is the same everywhere here. Raising net.core.rmem_max does not
-- change it -- that is a ceiling on what a program may request, and a UDP
-- socket takes the default unless it asks for more.
JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT run_id, scenario_name, provider FROM network_latency) s
ON s.run_id = sk.run_id AND s.scenario_name = sk.scenario_name

sql_code: -- One point per repetition: how much of the offered load arrived, as CPU
-- Placement is fixed and offered rate is faceted, because both affect
-- delivery far more than contention does.
-- TCP holds 100% at every steal level: its receive window throttles the
-- sender when the receiver stalls, so contention costs it delay rather than
-- data. UDP has no such feedback and turns the same stall into loss.
ORDER BY provider, protocol, offered_mps, steal_pct

sql_code: -- Ping-pong keeps one message in flight and waits for each reply. Under-load
-- sends at a fixed rate regardless of what comes back. At 1,000 messages per
-- second the load is low enough that both should agree, so whatever they
-- disagree by is the instrument rather than the network.
-- understatement_x is under-load divided by ping-pong: 1.0 means they agree,
-- above 1.0 means ping-pong reported the smaller number.
-- Ping-pong is self-clocked -- the next send waits for the previous reply --
-- so when the receiver stalls it sends nothing and records one delayed
-- sample. A fixed-rate sender keeps going, and every message sent during the
-- stall queues behind the ones before it. The same stall costs the closed
-- loop a single sample and the open loop as many as the stall was long. A
-- self-clocked measurement stops sampling exactly when the system is slow.
-- That is why the gap sits in the tail rather than the median: most samples
-- are still taken while things are healthy. It is widest where CPU steal is
-- highest, but stays above 1 even at zero steal, where a fixed-rate sender
round(median(CASE WHEN mode = 'pp' THEN p50_rtt_us END), 1)                        AS pingpong_p50_us,
round(median(CASE WHEN mode = 'ul' AND offered_mps = 1000 THEN p50_rtt_us END), 1) AS underload_1k_p50_us,
round(median(CASE WHEN mode = 'pp' THEN p99_rtt_us END), 1)                        AS pingpong_p99_us,
round(median(CASE WHEN mode = 'ul' AND offered_mps = 1000 THEN p99_rtt_us END), 1) AS underload_1k_p99_us,
SELECT provider, placement_class, protocol, 'p50' AS percentile,
ORDER BY percentile, provider, placement_class, protocol
r_code: to_svg <- svgstring(width = output.width.inch, height = output.height.inch, scaling = 1)
### the current table is bound to the variable 'df'
### The reference line is the whole point: 1.0 is where the two operating
### points agree, so distance from it is the size of the measurement artefact.
output <- ggplot(df, aes(x = placement_class, y = understatement_x, fill = protocol)) +
geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
facet_grid(percentile ~ provider) +
labs(x = NULL,
y = "under-load / ping-pong  (1.0 = the two agree)", fill = "Protocol",
subtitle = "Above 1.0, ping-pong reported a smaller number than a fixed-rate sender saw.") +
theme_bw() +
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
plot(output); dev.off(); to_svg() # output to the html page
